\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{गिरिः} (giriḥ)}{गिरिः (giriḥ)}]{\sk{गिरिः} (giriḥ) — a mountain, a hill}

\label{lesson:SA-C110-girih}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a lemon, then the Sanskrit for a cake.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{गिरिः}}
\textbf{\sk{गिरिः}} — \emph{giriḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a mountain, a hill\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{giri} \textquotedblleft{}a mountain, a hill\textquotedblright{} is inherited from Indo-European (EtymDB). MW sets it beside Avestan \emph{gairi} \textquotedblleft{}mountain\textquotedblright{}, and Old Church Slavonic \emph{gora} \textquotedblleft{}mountain\textquotedblright{}, still the Russian word, is a cousin (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{giriḥ}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} say \emph{giriḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a lemon, then the Sanskrit for a cake, then say \emph{giriḥ} again
\end{itemize}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{प्रपातः} (prapātaḥ)}{प्रपातः (prapātaḥ)}]{\sk{प्रपातः} (prapātaḥ) — a waterfall}

\label{lesson:SA-C110-prapatah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a cake, then the Sanskrit for a mountain.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{प्रपातः}}
\textbf{\sk{प्रपातः}} — \emph{prapātaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a waterfall\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{prapāta} comes from \emph{pra-√pat} \textquotedblleft{}fly forth, fall down\textquotedblright{}, the root √pat \textquotedblleft{}fall, fly\textquotedblright{} with \emph{pra} \textquotedblleft{}forth\textquotedblright{} (MW): \textquotedblleft{}a fall, a precipice\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 8682), and so a waterfall.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for this chapter.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Sanskrit for a cake, then the Sanskrit for a mountain, then say \emph{prapātaḥ} again

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{तरंगः} (taraṅgaḥ)}{तरंगः (taraṅgaḥ)}]{\sk{तरंगः} (taraṅgaḥ) — a wave}

\label{lesson:SA-C110-tarangah}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a mountain, then the Sanskrit for a waterfall.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{तरंगः}}
\textbf{\sk{तरंगः}} — \emph{taraṅgaḥ} — \textquotedblleft{}a wave\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{taraṅga} is built from \emph{taram} \textquotedblleft{}across\textquotedblright{}, from the root √tṝ \textquotedblleft{}cross\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{-ga} \textquotedblleft{}going\textquotedblright{}: MW explains it as \textquotedblleft{}the across-goer\textquotedblright{}, a wave. Punjabi kept it as \emph{taraṅg} \textquotedblleft{}wave\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 5699).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{विद्युत्} (vidyut)}{विद्युत् (vidyut)}]{\sk{विद्युत्} (vidyut) — lightning}

\label{lesson:SA-C110-vidyut}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a waterfall, then the Sanskrit for a wave.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{विद्युत्}}
\textbf{\sk{विद्युत्}} — \emph{vidyut} — \textquotedblleft{}lightning\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{vidyut} comes from \emph{vi-√dyut} \textquotedblleft{}flash forth\textquotedblright{}, the root √dyut \textquotedblleft{}shine\textquotedblright{} with \emph{vi-} \textquotedblleft{}out, apart\textquotedblright{} (MW): \textquotedblleft{}the flashing one\textquotedblright{}, lightning (CDIAL 11742). It lives on as Marathi and Gujarati \emph{vīj} \textquotedblleft{}lightning\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 11742).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\sk{गर्जनम्} (garjanam)}{गर्जनम् (garjanam)}]{\sk{गर्जनम्} (garjanam) — thunder}

\label{lesson:SA-C110-garjanam}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Sanskrit for a wave, then the Sanskrit for lightning.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{गर्जनम्}}
\textbf{\sk{गर्जनम्}} — \emph{garjanam} — \textquotedblleft{}thunder\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{garjana} \textquotedblleft{}roaring, thundering\textquotedblright{} comes from the root √garj \textquotedblleft{}roar, growl\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 4047), which MW compares with Latin \emph{garrire} \textquotedblleft{}chatter\textquotedblright{}, the source of English \emph{garrulous}. It lives on as Hindi \emph{gājan} \textquotedblleft{}thunder\textquotedblright{} (CDIAL 4047).
\end{cousinweb}
